chunks: Aḥmad ibn Muḥammad narrated from al-Walīd ibn Abān, who said:

I said to al-Riḍā عليه السلام: May I perform salat (prayer) in al-fanak and al-sinjāb? He said: “Yes.” Then I said: May one perform salat (prayer) in fox furs if they are properly slaughtered? He said: “Do not perform salat (prayer) in them.”
Al-Shaykh, may Allah have mercy on him, said: Salat (prayer) is not permissible for men in pure silk when there is choice, nor is wearing it permissible except in a state of necessity.
Muḥammad ibn Yaʿqūb narrated from Aḥmad ibn Idrīs, from Muḥammad ibn ʿAbd al-Jabbār, who said:
I wrote to Abī Muḥammad عليه السلام asking him: May salat (prayer) be performed in a cap of pure silk or a cap of dībāj? So he wrote: “Salat (prayer) is not lawful in pure silk.”

key_terms.الثَّعَالِبِ: fox furs, ruled here as not permissible for salat (prayer)
key_terms.السِّنْجَابِ: squirrel fur, mentioned here as permissible for salat (prayer)
key_terms.الِاضْطِرَارِ: a state of necessity or compulsion
key_terms.الْإِبْرِيسَمِ الْمَحْضِ: pure silk, prohibited for men in salat (prayer)
key_terms.الْفَنَكِ: a type of fur regarded here as permissible for salat (prayer)
key_terms.ذَكِيَّةً: properly slaughtered according to religious law
key_terms.قَلَنْسُوَةِ: a cap worn on the head

ai.seo_question: Can men perform salat (prayer) in animal fur or pure silk according to Shia hadith?
ai.summary: This hadith discusses legal rulings regarding clothing in salat (prayer), distinguishing between certain animal furs and prohibiting prayer in others. It also states that men may not perform salat (prayer) in pure silk, and wearing pure silk is only allowed in cases of necessity.
